# 6. Honoured Ancestors

*Pages PDF 133-142*

I IVI **II** 

## **Honoured Ancestors**
Belief in DwaRf society 

Manling religion is largely based on appeasing or appealing to their deities through prayer, ritual offerings, wearing symbols or charms, and (so they believe) tithing to the cult temples. Manlings do so in the hope their uncaring deities might show them favour or bestow a blessing. 

Dwarf beliefs are more concerned with venerating the Ancestor Gods rather than worshipping them. Temple services are more of a time of reflection for Dwarfs, granting the opportunity to honour the traditions set forth by the Ancestor Gods. Dwarfs visit the temple when they can, or on days that hold special meaning to them or their clan. Holy days are different as the entire Dwarf hold (except the garrison and mine patrols) gathers for the celebrations. Dwarf Priests and Loremasters use the festivities to recite the stories and reiterate the traditions laid down by the Ancestor Gods millennia ago. Outside Dwarf holds, such celebrations are more modest affairs, usually involving only the local Dwarf community. 

Dwarfs believe in a spirit world beneath the roots of the mountains where the Ancestor Gods rule and the spirits of their clan ancestors reside (called ‘Hall of Ancestors’ or _Gromthikhaz_ ). They also hold that the spirit world is close enough for the ancestors to watch over them, judge their achievements, and determine if they have lived honourable lives. Dwarfs do not believe the ancestors intervene in any meaningful way, which is fine with them. After all, it is up to the Dwarf to succeed in whatever task they have set for themselves. 

Dwarfs tend towards pragmatism, and they see little benefit in displaying symbols of the Ancestor Gods, save where it would honour them, and do not believe in the power of superstitious charms. Dwarfs certainly do not believe in the manling practice of Dooming or the (unseemly) fixation with Star Signs and discount most prophecy out of hand, save that credited to the keen insight of the Ancestors. 

## **The Ancestor Gods**
The most revered and important of the Ancestor Gods are Grungni, Valaya, and Grimnir, founders of Dwarf civilisation and most of its traditions. 

Grungni is the first of the Ancestor Gods to rise and the principal deity of the Dwarf pantheon. He taught the Dwarfs many of the skills for which they are famous: brewing, mining, metalwork, stonework, and weaponcraft. According to Dwarf lore, Grungni crafted some of the most powerful Dwarf artefacts. He also established Dwarf Law. Grungni was the one who foresaw the coming of Chaos and led the Dwarfs into the safety of the earth.  When the time was right, Grungni brought forth the Dwarf armies from their underground sanctuaries to battle the forces of Chaos. 

Valaya was the second Ancestor God to arise. She is the Ancestor God of the hearth and hold, whose domains include healing, sustenance, protection and strong dwellings. Valaya established much of Dwarf culture, and developed the runic script. As protector of the Dwarfs, Valaya devised a special rune to protect the Dwarfs in their underground refuge from the fell power of Chaos. While Dwarfs making war beyond the hold might raise their hammers to Grungni, those defending hearth and hold roar warcries to Valaya as they seek to protect their home. 

Brother to Grungni, Grimnir is the Ancestor God of warfare and warriors. Grimnir protected the Dwarfs from threats like Giants, Dragons, and Trolls during the time when the Dwarfs began to spread northwards along the World’s Edge Mountains. He also slaughtered great numbers of Chaos invaders with two mighty axes forged by Grungni. When Grimnir decided to find the ruptured Warpgate and close it, he created the ritual that Slayers follow today. 

I IVI **II** 

The Ancestor God shaved his hair except for a crest he dyed orange and spiked with animal fat. Grimnir then tattooed his entire body with elaborate patterns and included his personal rune before departing without ceremony. Today, dishonoured Dwarfs entering the Slayer cult follow the Ancestor God’s final ritual. 

The last Ancestor God to rise was Gazul, brother to the Grungni, Valaya, and Grimnir. Protector of the Dead, Gazul established the Dwarf tradition of venerating their ancestors, whether living or dead. Embracing his role, Gazul left no descendants and established the ritual of burial which assisted the departed’s spirit transition to the spirit world. Whilst Gazul may be considered alongside Grungni, Valaya, and Grimnir in terms of his age, he is not held in the hearts and minds of Dwarfs to the same degree of fondness. For all the importance of his role in managing the realm of the Dwarf dead he is considered somehow lesser to the main three Ancestor Gods. 

The Shaper of Ore, Smednir was the first of the second generation of Ancestor Gods and son of Grungni and Valaya. Learning from his father, Smednir took the art of metalcraft, jewelcraft, and refining ore to new heights. Smednir elevated Dwarf craftsmanship. 

Thungni is the younger son of Grungni and Valaya. He is the Ancestor God of Runic Magic and Runesmithing. According to Dwarf legend, Thungni ventured deep into the earth before the Dwarf ’s spread from the south of the World’s Edge Mountains and spent considerable time in a place he called _Ankor Bryn_ (‘Glittering Realm’). When he returned, Thungni brought the secrets of Runic Magic to the Dwarfs. Legends further tell of Thungni learning craftsmanship and metalworking from his brother, Smednir. Together, the two brothers crafted most of the great runic weapons of the Dwarf Ancestor Gods and the future legendary Dwarf kings. In time, Thungni learned that only he and his future descendants had the gift to inscribe Runic Magic. 

The first Dwarf engineer, Morgrim was the last of the second generation of Ancestor Gods, the son of Grimnir. He developed the techniques of crafting engines of war and other non-military devices. During the Coming of Chaos, Morgrim’s creations gave the Dwarfs an edge in fighting the vast Chaos armies. He later joined Grimnir’s journey to the north, but was turned back by his father before Grimnir entered the Chaos Wastes. 

With the closing of the Warpgate and the creation of the Vortex, the three-millennia-long Time of the Ancestor Gods was over. Grungni and Valaya were the first to descend into the deep earth where they found their way to the Hall of Ancestors with Gazul’s help and joined the spirits of the Dwarfs who departed before them. Smednir, Thungni, and Morgrim soon made their own journey to the deep in the company of Gazul. 

Before his final departure, Gazul travelled to each Dwarf hold to train a priesthood dedicated to each of the Ancestor Gods, including himself. Their task was to ensure that Dwarfs remained true to the traditions laid down by the Ancestor Gods and to one another. Once his task, Gazul himself journeyed to the deep so he too could join his brethren in the Hall of Ancestors. 

## **The Priesthood**
When forming the priesthood for the Ancestor Gods, Gazul selected members of the Runesmith clan to undertake this critical role. He foresaw the need for the priesthood to have some ability to craft magic runes and deliberately chose those of limited ability. Gazul knew that the few Runesmiths with greater ability needed to focus on their craft without undue distractions. 

Belief is integral to Dwarf society as it transcends the normal bounds dictated by clan and, to a lesser extent, craft guild. Priests are held in high esteem, both for their wisdom and representation of the Ancestor Gods. They play a major role in the cohesion of Dwarf society. Mediation by priests have settled disputes between clans, as well as between Dwarf holds. Priests have also played a part in the application of Dwarf law. 

Unlike manling priests, Dwarf priests do not wear ostentatious robes, outsized and ornate religious symbols, badges of office, or carry books of prayer. They wear simple garb, much like that of a typical craft Dwarf. Symbols denoting their office are usually worn on the outside. The medallions are modest affairs, usually made of silver with the Ancestor God’s rune or symbol inscribed. 

Dwarf priests can inscribe Runic Magic of limited power. The collection of available Runes is specific to the Ancestor God of the priest. Taught to the novice priest during the latter years of their apprenticeship. Apprentice priests must successfully undergo a rite that elevates them to priesthood before they are able to inscribe runic magic. Dwarf priests cannot create new magic runes. 

I IVI **II** 

While the individual Ancestor Gods have their own dedicated priesthood, there is no rivalry between them like what exists with manlings (for example, Sigmar and Ulric). No Dwarf priest disrespects their counterpart, knowing that Dwarfs venerate all the Ancestor Gods. In fact, all Dwarf priests celebrate each Ancestor God’s holy days with their fellow Dwarfs. 

The manling religious concept of penance is another thing lost on Dwarf priests. The Dwarf sense of honour precludes the priest from undertaking any act that would go against the strictures of the Ancestor Gods to whom they represent. After all, there is but one path forward for Dwarfs who dishonoured themselves and their clan — that of the Slayer. 

## **Travelling Priests**
Most Dwarf priests are tied to the Ancestor God Temple of their resident Dwarf hold where they perform the expected services for resident Dwarfs. The only time Dwarf hold priests depart the confines of the holds occurs when they are selected to travel with military expeditions. Many Karak and Norse Dwarfs inhabit mountain settlements outside the Dwarf Holds. Fortified towns in the Dwarf realm usually have small temples to Grungni and Valaya and Gazul burial vaults to which Dwarf priests are permanently assigned. 

Dwarfs in smaller settlements (trading posts, villages, hamlets, farmsteads, fortified inns, and mines) depend on travelling priests. These priests, particularly those for Grungni and Gazul, make the rounds administering services to the scattered Dwarfs. An itinerant priest’s routes and schedules are well-known to the populace so any divergence from such could easily result in search parties. The smaller communities have underground shrines and burial vaults where itinerant priests can conduct services. 

In the manling realms, Grungni priests support all the religious needs that are usually undertaken by the other Ancestor Gods. The only exceptions to this are the tasks usually assigned to Gazul priests as these involve the important work of tending to the dying and burying the dead. Large cities and towns have fixed underground temples and burial vaults. Yet, many Imperial Dwarfs reside in villages and hamlets. Itinerant priests of Grungni and Gazul travel together with one or two Dwarf guards in a fixed circuit to these smaller settlements. The company usually resides for a specified time with the most prominent Imperial Dwarf in the village. 

## **Dwarf Calendar**
The widely used Imperial calendar is based primarily on the Dwarf calendar. One of main differences between the two, other than the names of the months and special days, is that the Dwarfs do not distinguish the days of the week. To a Dwarf, every day is a workday except for the Ancestor Gods’ holy days. The Dwarf calendar counts its years from the time Karaz-a-Karak was established as capital of Karaz Ankor. This event occurred 4500 years before the crowning of Sigmar as Emperor. Imperial Dwarfs use the Imperial calendar. 

The Day of Remembrance is one of the most important days among Dwarfs. There is no set date as each Dwarf kingdom celebrates the day on a date that is significant to that Dwarf kingdom. Imperial Dwarf clans set their own date based on an event important to that clan. If there are many clans in a large Imperial settlement, such as Altdorf, then the clan elders come to an agreement as to when the day should be celebrated.

I IVI **II** 

## **Temples and Shrines**
Every Dwarf hold has individual temples to the Ancestor Gods. In some Dwarf holds, special favour may be bestowed on one Ancestor God over the others due to that Hold’s history and traditions. That recognition does not translate into bias, however. It just simply means that the emphasis of a particular Dwarf hold can be determined by the size of a particular Ancestor God’s example. For instance, Karak Azul built the largest temple of Grungni in recognition of it being the greatest metalworking centre of Karaz Ankor. 

Dwarf hold temples are massive halls with vaulted ceilings intended for large attendance during festive holy days. The temples rival the size of a Dwarf king’s audience hall. Temples are very well-lit with interior walls typically decorated with some sort of depiction of the Ancestor God or their deeds. A lectern from which the High Priest addresses the gathering stands on a dais opposite the temple’s entrance. 

Small underground temples to Grungni are found in the smaller settlements, trading posts, mines, and fortified inns within a Dwarf kingdom. These temples have individual shrines to the other two principal Ancestor Gods, Valaya and Grimnir. All have underground burial vaults where priests of Gazul perform the burial rites before interring the dead. 

Only Grungni temples are found within the Dwarf quarters of manling cities and large towns. These temples are built underground and often have passageways to underground vaults where priests of Gazul hold sway. Statues of Gazul are often the only marker indicating his domain. Within its walls, temples of Grungni have shrines for Valaya and Grimnir. 

Imperial Dwarf history has some darker moments where relationships with manlings were strained. As a result, many Dwarf temples are heavily fortified with secret doors leading to subterranean escape routes unknown to manlings. Imperial Dwarfs take nothing for chance. 

Where Imperial Dwarfs are scattered in villages and hamlets in a specific area, there are only shrines to the Grungni and Valaya (sometimes Grimnir) within the cellars of their homes. The largest of the settlements in that area will have a stone cellar beneath the largest Dwarf establishment (most often an inn or smithy) where Imperial Dwarfs can gather away from prying eyes to celebrate the main Ancestor Gods. Underground tunnels from these secret halls lead to subterranean vaults where the dead are interred by wandering Gazul priests. 

## **Dwarf Cult Descriptions**
Dwarf Ancestor God cults are not hierarchical in the same sense as the Cult of Sigmar. There is no supreme head of the cult. Each temple in a Dwarf hold or large Imperial Dwarf community is independently run by the hierarchy of priests within that temple. The only unifying feature for the Dwarfs is that the entire priesthood are members of the tradition-minded Runesmith clans. 

Due to the independent nature of each Ancestor God Temple, there is little need for a similar division of the Cult (‘Orders’) that focuses on a single aspect of the deity. Dwarfs tend to see this aspect of manling religion baffling. 

Dwarf belief embraces an oral tradition. Stories and traditions are passed from one generation to another by Priests during the holy day celebrations. Holy texts are not as apparent in Dwarf culture as that of manling faith. Nevertheless, each Dwarf priest, and may ordinary Dwarfs, can recount tales of the Ancestors for many hours, pausing only to take a respectful gulp of ale. 

I IVI **II** 

## **Grungni**
The interior of underground temples is lavishly decorated with carved scenes from ancient Dwarf myths. A large statue of Grungni with his pick-axe (sometimes, warhammer) stands at one end of the temple. Shrines tend to be more modest affairs with a small statue of Grungni. 

**Largest Temple:** Karak Azul 

**Major Festivals:** Every 100 days: 33 Pflugzeit (Barrel Making), 33 Vorgeheim (First Quaff), 33 Brauzeit (Second Breech), 33 Vorhexen (Keg End) 

**Common Holy Symbols:** Miner’s pickaxe, stylised depiction of a helmeted face with a long and forked beard, Grungni’s rune 

## **Cult Runic Magic**
Priests of Grungni may inscribe the following runes: Alarm, Blasting, Enemy Detection, Forging, Furnace, Preservation, Purification, Verminkill, Warding, Warmth, Warning, and Water. 

Grungni is the first founding Ancestor God to rise and brother to Grimnir, and Gazul. He is portrayed as having a forked iron-grey beard that reaches his feet, and is normally depicted as carrying a large miner’s pick called _Blidazdurakaz_ (‘Lightning Pick-axe’). In his martial aspect, Grungni is armed with his runic warhammer, _Drongrundum_ (‘Thunder Hammer’). 

## **Strictures**

- Through the quality of your gem cutting, your smithing, your brewing, and your masonry, uphold the glory of clan and hold. 

## **Holy Sites**
Temples to Grungni can be found in every hold in the mountain realms and Norsca. They can also be found beneath cities and large towns in manling realms where a sizable Dwarf population exists. Smaller Dwarf settlements have underground shrines, usually located beneath an inn or smithy where Dwarfs congregate. 

- Strive to ensure that each passage and hallway you construct is sound enough to endure the ages. 

- By hammer and by hand, mend what is broken. 

- Extract from the ground all the riches that are given to the Dawi. 

Mines in the Dwarf kingdoms have their own shrine to Grungni, near the mine’s entrance. Dwarf breweries have shrines and a small statue of Grungni with two tankards of beer, one in each hand, in a prominent corner of the brewhouse. 

- Never squander the wealth gemstones and gold may grant you and your legacy. 

- Never surrender to Orcs, Goblins, or their kin. 

- Wherever our lands have fallen to our enemies, strive to reclaim them with axe and hammer. 

I IVI **II** 

## **Valaya**
**Largest Temple:** Karaz-a-Karak **Major Festivals:** Mitterfruhl ( _Materfran_ ) and Mittherbst ( _Materhazt_ ) 

Shrines to Valaya are also erected within all Grungni temples built outside Dwarf holds. The entrance of Dwarf hold libraries have statues of Valaya depicted with a stylus-chisel in one hand and an open book with foil pages in the other. These acknowledge Valaya’s role in developing picture runes ( _Agrurhun_ ) and the basic runic alphabet ( _Klinkarhun_ ) for writing. 

**Common Holy Symbols:** Shield with ‘Ancestor Queen’ ( _Gromthi Rinn_ ) runes, sheaf of hops or barley, stylised hearth, Valaya’s rune. 

Valaya is the second of the founding Ancestor Gods, wife of Grungni. All Dwarfs trace their ancestry to Valaya. In her usual depiction, Valaya is an archetypal Dwarf woman, proud, strong, of regal bearing with long, braided hair reaching to her feet. She is normally shown wearing a horned helmet and chain mail over a gown with gold trim. Valaya carries a rune-axe called _Kradskonti_ (‘Peacemaker’). 

## **Cult Runic Magic**
Priests of Valaya can inscribe the following runes: Alarm, Battle, Enemy Detection, Healing, Light, Preservation, Purification, Resistance, Restoration, Sanctuary, Silence, Slowness, Spell Breaking, Verminkill, Warmth, Warning, Water 

A High Priest of Valaya can also inscribe the Master Rune of Valaya. 

## **Holy Sites**
All Dwarf holds have temples to Valaya, usually placed between those of Grungni and Grimnir in the Deep of Renown, the area of the hold where shrines to the Ancestors and the vaulted halls of remembering can be found. The walls of her temples depict domestic scenes of Dwarf life in relief. Statues of Valaya flank the altar where Dwarfs make offerings to honour the Ancestor Goddess. The left statue depicts Valaya unarmoured with a healthy infant in one arm and a tankard of beer in the free hand. The right statue is of Valaya in her role as protector, wearing mail coat and helmet with a shield held before her and an axe raised high. 

## **Strictures**

- Always provide aid to a wounded or ailing Dawi. 

- Always assist a Dwarf-friend in need. 

- Always tend to the needs of the young Beardlings. 

- Defy our enemies in battle, defend your hold with honour. 

- Always keep ale and a warm fire for honoured guests. 

- Never allow the relics and treasures of our holds to fall into the hands of enemies, unless to do so saves Dawi lives. 

Temples of Valaya do not occur outside Dwarf holds. Instead, every Dwarf domicile has a shrine to Valaya. 

I IVI **II** 

## **Grimnir**
**Largest Temple:** Karak Kadrin **Major Festivals:** None **Common Holy Symbols:** Double-bladed axe, Grimnir’s rune 

Grimnir is known as the Ancestor God who aggressively protected the Dwarfs on the Long Migration and during the Coming of Chaos. He is often depicted as a powerfully-built Dwarf with an intense stare. There are two versions of Grimnir. The first is where the warrior Ancestor God is dressed in the ancient Dwarf armour with his mighty axes, _Az-Dreugidum_ (‘Waraxe of Doom’) and _Onkegruni_ (‘Widow-Maker’) raised for attack. The second, and more famous, Slayer depiction is of Grimnir’s bare chest and arms ritually scarred and elaborately tattooed, wearing the spiked orange crest typically seen with Slayers, and only wielding his remaining axe, _AzDreugidum_ . The second image represents his appearance as he entered the Chaos Wastes. 

## **Holy Sites**
Every Dwarf hold has a Grimnir temple, most of which depict the Ancestor God as the armoured fighter with two axes. The largest of these temples is in Karaz-aKarak. The largest temple to Grimnir, however, is the one in Karak Kadrin built within Slayers’ Hall in which he appears as the Slayer he was at the end. There is a second temple to Grimnir in Karak Kadrin where he is depicted as he is in other Dwarf Holds. As only Slayers may enter Slayers’ Hall, the temple opened to the rest of the Kadrin Dwarfs is found in the Deep of Renown among the temples of the other Ancestor Gods. 

Slayers’ Hall and its temple are built in a cordoned off section of Upper Deep to keep dishonoured Slayers away from the rest of the populace. The Slayer King frequents the temple at Slayers’ Hall. 

The interior walls of Grimnir the Warrior temples depict scenes where fully-armoured Grimnir battles fierce monsters during the Long Migration and twisted Chaos warriors erupting from the Coming of Chaos in relief. The focus of the relief scenes on walls in the Grimnir the Slayer temple involve his journey as a Slayer to the Chaos Wastes as told by his son, Morgrim. 

Shrines to Grimnir the Warrior exist in every barracks where Dawi warriors gather. Similar shrines exist in Imperial Dwarf temples dedicated to Grungni. 

## **Cult Runic Magic**
Priests of Grimnir can inscribe the following runes: Battle, Breaking, Clear Seeing, Cleaving, Courage, Cutting, Farseeing, Fear, Fury, Might, Signalling, Silence, Slowness, Smiting, Striking, Warning 

## **Strictures**

- Obey the command of the Longbeards. 

- Stand solid as stone before the brutal foe and do not retire from the field of battle until its end. 

- Slay the enemies of the Dawi wherever you may find them. 

- Strive to slay monstrous foes of the Dawi wherever they encroach on our holds and deeps. 

I IVI **II** 

## **Gazul**
**Largest Temple:** Karaz-a-Karak **Major Festivals:** None 

**Common Holy Symbols:** Stylised cave entrance, flame, Gazul’s rune 

The youngest brother of the Ancestor Gods to arise, Gazul has long brooded over the mortality of his kin. To ensure that the spirits of the Dwarfs would not be lost, Gazul created the Hall of Ancestors in the spirit world beneath the mountains for the Dawi to reside when their bodies die. He also created the Ritual of Passage ( _Durugenritak_ ). 

Gazul is often depicted as a gloomy Dwarf with sad eyes and grim demeanour. He has a pale complexion that contrasts with his jet black hair and beard, both of which have streaks of grey, especially at the temples and corner of the mouth. Gazul wears black armour under a black cloak, and carries a great runesword named _Zharrvengryn_ (‘Flaming Death’). 

## **Smednir**
**Largest Temple:** Karak Azul **Major Festivals:** Hexenstag ( _Hekesdeg_ ) **Common Holy Symbols:** Anvil, Smednir’s rune 

As the older son of Grungni and Valaya, Smednir is credited by legend to elevating the workmanship expected of Dwarfs in the areas of the refining of ore and metalworking from that of meeting practical needs with crafting works of art, particularly precious metals. Smednir also developed and taught the skills of effectively refining and working with gromril, the hardest metal in the world. 

Smednir is depicted as a bare-armed, muscular Dwarf wearing a leather apron with his single-plait, braided beard thrown over his shoulder and away from a forge’s flames. Smednir grips tongs holding a metal piece in his left hand while holding on to his runic hammer _Azulokrid_ (‘Metal Crafter’) in his right. 

## **Holy Sites**
## **Holy Sites**
Every Dwarf hold has a Temple to Gazul, but these are not found with other Ancestor God temples in the Deep of Renown. Gazul Temples are found in the Deep of Gazul along with the many burial vaults and preparation rooms the cult administers. Ogre-sized statues of solemn-looking Gazul guard the entrance to his temples and burial vaults. A small altar stands in the middle of the temple where those honouring the recently dead can likewise honour Gazul. Outside the Dwarf holds, Dwarf burial vaults are often attached by tunnels to a temple to Grungni. A shrine to Gazul with a small statue of Gazul nearby is built near the opening of the entrance tunnel. For larger settlements, like Imperial cities, a Gazul priest is permanently assigned to that location.  Smaller settlements depend on an itinerant Gazul priest. Preparation rooms are located near the shrine. 

## **Strictures**

- Defy the tomb robber, ghoul, and necromancer, for they are enemies to be despised. 

- Honour our dead, protect their spirits and guard their reputations. 

Every Dwarf hold has a temple to Smednir decorated with scenes of the ancestor working in a smithy or refining ore are depicted in bas-relief on the interior walls. Shrines to Smednir are found in all Dwarf kingdom smithing workshops, stamp mills, and smelters. Shrines also exist in the workshops, mills, and smelters where Imperial Dwarfs run these enterprises. Dwarf smelters and smiths gather at Smednir holy sites at the turn of the year to celebrate the completion of old work and beginning of new. 

## **Cult Runic Magic**
Priests of Smednir may inscribe the following runes: Cleaving, Cutting, Fate, Fire, Forging, Furnace, Iron, Silence, Smiting 

## **Strictures**
   - Strive always to produce your best work. 

   - Labour not for those unworthy of the craft of the Dawi. 

   - Prize and protect your tools and forge as you would your greatest treasure. 

- Respect the dignity of the ancestors, to disturb their resting places is a heavy matter. 

I IVI **II** 

## **Thungni**
## **Largest Temple:** Karaz-A-Karak
## **Major Festivals:** None
**Common Holy Symbols:** Thungni’s rune on a hammer Thungni is the younger son of Grungni and Valaya who learned metalcraft from his brother Smednir. The two _Ankor_ brothers worked together after Thungni’s return from _Bryn_ to craft some of the earliest and best known runic weapons. As progenitor of the Runesmith clans, taught his early descendants the secret knowledge of runesmithing. 

Thungni is portrayed as an elated Dwarf with bronzecoloured hair and beard. He is clad in full armour with his personal rune inscribed on the breastplate. Thungni holds a runic staff in his raised left hand symbolising his power and mastery of runesmithing. He holds the runic hammer, _Karaz-Kazakrhun_ (‘Enduring War Rune’) in his relaxed right hand. 

## **Holy Sites**
Temples of Thungni are only found in Dwarf holds with the largest in Karaz-a-Karak.  A second, smaller temple in Karaz-a-Karak is found within _Rhunriken Ankor_ (‘Runesmith’s Lair’) where Master Runelord Kragg the Grimm power is unrivalled. The walls of Thungni temples have frescos illustrating Thungni’s journey to the Glittering Realm and his triumphant return. A giant statue of Thungni stands proud upon the dais located near the rear of the temple. There are no shrines to Thungni outside the Dwarf holds, not even in the manling lands. 

## **Cult Runic Magic**
Priests of Thungni rarely inscribe runes, leaving such tasks to runesmiths. Should there be a need, priests are restricted to the following: 

Alarm, Communication, Disclosure, Enemy Detection, Luck, Sanctuary 

## **Morgrim**
## **Largest Temple:** Zhufbar **Major Festivals:** Sonnstill ( _Zhomerstikul_ )
**Common Holy Symbols:** Stylised stone thrower, rope and pulley, Morgim’s rune 

Morgrim is the son of Grimnir and Valaya and the first Dwarf engineer. After Grungni’s warning of the Coming of Chaos, Morgrim and his clan crafted bolt and stone throwers of all sizes. They also devised traps to form the first line of defence against the invading hordes. Morgrim journeyed part way to the Chaos Wastes with Grimnir, but his father bade his son to return with one of his signature axes to ensure the continued aggressive defence of the Dwarfs until the Warpgate was closed. Morgrim is usually portrayed as a mail-clad Dwarf wearing a belt hung with tools typical of a Dwarf engineer. In most depictions, Morgrim has dust in his hair and beard with his hands covered in grease. He carries one of his father’s axes, _Onkegruni_ (‘Widow-Maker’). 

## **Holy Sites**
All Dwarf holds have a temple to Morgrim in the Deep of Renown with the largest in Zhufbar, the most industrialised of all Dwarf holds. Two statues of Morgrim standing proud guard the entrance to his temple. Most temples display frescos of the various war machines associated with the Engineers craft guild. In contrast, the Barak Varr temple displays the various warships for which that Hold is renowned. Shrines to Morgrim exist in the Engineer Guildhall in the Royal Deep as well as beneath the Dwarf Engineers Guilds in the Empire. 

## **Cult Runic Magic**
Priests of Morgrim may inscribe the following runes: Accuracy, Alarm, Burning, Clear Seeing, Disguise, Enemy Detection, Farseeing, Forging, Fortune, Furnace, Immolation, Penetrating, Reloading, Seeking, Signalling 

## **Strictures**

- Treasure the secrets of runecraft as carefully as you treasure gold. 

- Sooner see your work destroyed than fall into enemy hands. 

- Reclaim those items of runecraft that are wielded by those unworthy of them. 

- Where our secrets are possessed by those unworthy of them, see to it that our secrets perish with them . 

- You will be judged by your work, so strive to be the best. 

High Priests of Morgrim may inscribe the Master Rune of Defence. 

## **Strictures**

- Always seek redress from those who steal our secrets. 

- Make your craft precise, and effective in its function. 

- Innovate, but be cautious as you go. Ambition should not come at the detriment of craft. 

- All engineering knowledge is sacred and must be preserved, even at the cost of novel concepts. 

- All construction phases of an engineer’s craft must be accompanied by the recital of the appropriate Guild litany. 

I IVI **II** 

## **Ancestor Veneration**
For Dwarfs, the veneration of one’s ancestors is equal to that honouring the Ancestor Gods. Such adoration does not require Ancestor God priests to be present. Venerating one’s ancestors can be undertaken by an individual, with family, or with the entire clan. The place to honour one’s ancestors can also vary. This can be done in the home, a clan hall, on the battlefield, or even in a taproom with one’s mates. Moreover, it can be done at any time of the day. 

Dwarfs know that they are part of the unbroken chain with their ancestors. They keep the ancestors foremost in their mind whenever they find themselves at crucial crossroads in their lives. Dwarfs often think of ancestors when they need to make life-altering decisions, often debating which path would honour the ancestors or shame them. In such situations, Dwarfs weigh their own personal experiences with that of ancestors whose stories entail similar dilemmas. 

Manling companions may think Dwarfs too obsessive when it comes to their ancestors, but manlings are generally too rash and self-centred to properly consider consequences. 

## **Honouring the Ancestors**
Dwarfs are usually very regimented in how they conduct themselves from day to day. When it comes to venerating ancestors, Dwarfs are very individualistic in their approach. 

One of the common ways Dwarfs honour ancestors happens when a clan gathers to recite the deeds of their long-lost kin through storytelling or song. The ‘Saga of Gotrek Gotreksson and the Recovery of Kazad Bebbanberk” takes the _Kolgrund_ (‘Black Hammer’) brewing clan of Kraka Ravnsvake several hours to relate the tale, usually in song, while drinking copious amounts of ale and mead throughout. Giving thanks to ancestors is an example of a more reflective method of veneration. Rorek Duraksson, an Ubersreik smith in good standing, starts his day with morning devotions offering thanks to ancestors for providing him with another day to honour them through his craft. 

Most of the time, ancestor veneration falls between the above two examples. Many families call a gathering to commemorate ancestors. For example, Turstan Silverbeard of the _Agrilhandaz_ (‘Silver Hand’) clan, one of two Silversmith Guildmasters in Meissen (the other is a 

manling), invites his children and their families to gather at his spacious townhouse in the Silberkelch district to honour family ancestors. Turstan’s son, Bronn, lives in the nearby village of Dornstadt with his wife. Turstan’s daughter, Freda, and her family reside further away in Willstätter. When gathered, Turstan and his family share stories of ancestors (including those of his children’s spouses) as they venerate their respective forebears all night long over beer and a hearty meal. 

## **Strictures**

- Always honour one’s ancestors on every Day of Remembrance. 

- Never perform or permit an act that brings dishonour to the memory of a clan ancestor. 

- Always seek the guidance of an ancestor before any great undertaking. 

## **Clan Shrines and Traditions**
Clan shrines and traditions are as varied as the clans who venerate their ancestors. All clanhalls and family dwellings have shrines dedicated to clan ancestors. 

A shrine’s location within a home or clanhall varies from one family to the next, one clan to another. Sometimes they are conspicuously placed in a common area where members gather. Other times, shrines are positioned in a more private area for personal reflection. 

A shrine’s structure also varies. They may be as simple as a small table with a tankard of Dwarf beer and some other symbol of the clan’s or family’s craft. More elaborate shrines have portraits of a few ancestors and, possibly, an ancestor’s personal possession or two prominently displayed. In some dwellings, the shrine of ancestors stands near the shrines dedicated to Ancestor Gods. 

While there are no holy days as such for ancestor veneration, members of a clan gather on that clan’s designated Day of Remembrance to share stories of the ancestors and comment upon the lessons the tale is conveying to the living. These accounts vary from solemn accounts to humorous stories to cautionary tales. Remembering the ancestors can be both joyous and sad, enlightening and entertaining, or just simply informative. 

In addition to the clan’s day, Individual Dwarf families have their own Day of Remembrance, particularly for recently deceased ancestors. In such cases, tokens of the newly buried ancestors are added to the family’s shrine.
